claim: Forty-six right-handed individuals (27 females, aged 18–28 years) participated in the MRI study.
source: Forty-six right-handed individuals (27 females, aged 18–28 years) participated in the MRI study.
evidence: Directly stated demographic information about study participants.

claim: Ten individuals were removed from the final analysis due to excessive head motion in the MRI scanner, incomplete scans, poor task compliance, or missing data.
source: Of these 46 participants, 10 individuals were removed from the final analysis either due to excessive head motion in the MRI scanner, incomplete scans, poor task compliance (i.e., >25% of trials not being completed within the maximal trial duration), or missing data (i.e., >20% of trials being missed due to insufficient pressure of the fingertip on the MRI-compatible tablet).
evidence: Directly stated exclusion criteria and number of excluded participants.

claim: The final sample size for analysis was 36 participants.
source: Forty-six right-handed individuals (27 females, aged 18–28 years) participated in the MRI study. Of these 46 participants, 10 individuals were removed from the final analysis
evidence: Calculated from 46 initial participants minus 10 excluded participants, and confirmed by N=36 notation throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Queen's University Research Ethics Board approved the study with ethics approval number CNS-019-16.
source: The Queen's University Research Ethics Board approved the study (ethics approval number: CNS-019-16), and it was conducted in coherence to the principles outlined in the Canadian Tri-Council Policy Statement on Ethical Conduct for Research Involving Humans and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki (1964).
evidence: Directly stated ethics approval information.

claim: Participants performed a baseline block of 70 trials without receiving any feedback about their performance.
source: In the baseline block, participants did not receive any feedback about their performance.
evidence: Directly stated experimental condition.

claim: Participants performed a learning block of 200 trials in which they received score feedback (0-100 points) after each trial.
source: In the learning block, participants were rewarded 0–100 points after reaching the movement distance marker, and were instructed to do their best to maximize this score across trials
evidence: Directly stated experimental condition.

claim: Subjects could only use reward-based learning mechanisms and not error-based learning mechanisms because they received no visual feedback about their actual finger trajectory.
source: Importantly, because subjects received no visual feedback about their actual finger trajectory and could not see their own hand, they could only use the score feedback—and thus only reward-based learning mechanisms—to modify their movements from one trial to the next (Dam et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated reasoning about learning mechanisms with supporting citations.

claim: Error-based learning requires sensory errors that convey both the change in direction and magnitude needed to correct the movement.
source: That is, subjects could not use error-based learning mechanisms to achieve learning in our study as this form of learning requires sensory errors that convey both the change in direction and magnitude needed to correct the movement.
evidence: Directly stated definition of error-based learning requirements.

claim: Subjects on average were able to use the reward-based feedback to increase their score over the 200 learning trials.
source: As can be seen in Figure 1D, subjects on average were able to use the reward-based feedback to increase their score, and thus produce a trajectory more similar to the hidden path, over the 200 learning trials
evidence: Directly stated result with reference to Figure 1D showing learning curve.

claim: Three distinct, equal-length epochs were used to study changes in functional cortical and striatal organization: baseline (70 trials), early learning (initial 70 trials after reward feedback onset), and late learning (final 70 trials).
source: In order to study the changes in functional cortical and striatal organization during the learning task, we used three distinct, equal-length epochs over the time course of the study. Specifically, in addition to the task baseline epoch (70 trials), we defined early and late learning epochs as the subsequent initial and final 70 trials, respectively, following the presentation onset of reward feedback.
evidence: Directly stated epoch definitions for analysis.

claim: Mean BOLD time-series data were extracted for each cortical region defined by the Schaefer 1000 cortical parcellation.
source: For each participant, we extracted mean blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) time-series data for each cortical region defined by the Shaefer 1000 cortical parcellation (Schaefer et al., 2018)
evidence: Directly stated data extraction method with citation.

claim: Mean BOLD time-series data were extracted for striatal regions defined by the Harvard-Oxford parcellation.
source: and for striatal regions defined by the Harvard-Oxford parcellation (Avants et al., 2008; Frazier et al., 2005)
evidence: Directly stated data extraction method with citations.

claim: Covariance (functional connectivity) matrices were estimated for each epoch (baseline, early, and late).
source: and then estimated covariance (functional connectivity) matrices for each epoch (baseline, early, and late; Figure 1E; for a similar approach, see Gale et al., 2022).
evidence: Directly stated analysis method with figure reference and citation.

claim: Prior work suggests that individual differences in functional connectivity can obscure task-related effects.
source: Because prior work (Gordon et al., 2017; Gratton et al., 2018), including our own (Areshenkoff et al., 2022; Areshenkoff et al., 2021; Gale et al., 2022), suggests that individual differences in functional connectivity can obscure any task-related effects
evidence: Directly stated rationale with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Connectivity matrices were centered using the Riemannian manifold approach.
source: we centered the connectivity matrices using the Riemmanian manifold approach (Areshenkoff et al., 2022; Areshenkoff et al., 2021; Gale et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2018; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for an overview of the approach).
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing method with citations and figure reference.

claim: Prior to the centering procedure, covariance matrices mainly cluster according to subject identity.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, prior to the centering procedure the covariance matrices mainly cluster according to subject identity, consistent with prior findings showing that this subject-level structure explains the majority of the variance in functional connectivity data (Gratton et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated observation with figure reference and supporting citation.

claim: After applying the centering procedure, subject-level clustering is abolished.
source: However, after applying the centering procedure (Figure 2B), this subject-level clustering is abolished, potentially allowing for the differentiation of the three task-related epochs.
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: The top three principal components (PCs) of the template baseline manifold explain approximately 70% of the total variance.
source: Collectively, these top three PCs explain ~70% of the total variance (Figure 3B).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with figure reference.

claim: PC1 distinguishes visual regions (positive loadings) from somatomotor regions (negative loadings).
source: As can be seen in Figure 3A, PC1 distinguishes visual regions (positive loadings in red) from somatomotor regions (negative loadings in blue).
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: PC2 distinguishes visual and somatomotor regions from high-order association regions within the default mode network (DMN).
source: Meanwhile, PC2 distinguishes visual and somatomotor regions (in red) from the remaining cortical areas (in blue), most prominently high-order association regions within the DMN.
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: PC3 mainly constitutes a gradient of frontoparietal areas of the dorsal attention network (DAN) and frontoparietal control network (FCN) versus DMN regions.
source: Finally, PC3 mainly constitutes a gradient of frontoparietal areas of the dorsal attention network (DAN) and frontoparietal control network (FCN) versus DMN regions.
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: PCs 1 and 2 jointly differentiate visual, DMN, and somatomotor regions, replicating the tripartite structure of the brain's intrinsic functional architecture.
source: When we mapped the brain regions onto their assigned intrinsic functional network architecture (Thomas Yeo et al., 2011), we confirmed that PCs 1 and 2 jointly differentiate visual, DMN, and somatomotor regions, replicating the tripartite structure of the brain's intrinsic functional architecture (Huntenburg et al., 2018; Margulies et al., 2016; Figure 3D).
evidence: Directly stated result with citations and figure reference.

claim: The tripartite structure is a fundamental feature of functional brain organization, whereby the transition from unimodal cortex to transmodal cortex reflects a global processing hierarchy from lower- to higher-order brain systems.
source: Others have argued that this tripartite structure is a fundamental feature of functional brain organization, whereby the transition from unimodal cortex (visual and somatomotor networks) to transmodal cortex (the DMN) reflects a global processing hierarchy from lower- to higher-order brain systems (Huntenburg et al., 2018; Margulies et al., 2016; Smallwood et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: Manifold eccentricity is computed as the Euclidean distance from the manifold centroid.
source: we computed the manifold eccentricity of each region by taking its Euclidean distance from manifold centroid (coordinates (0,0,0); see Figure 3E).
evidence: Directly stated method with figure reference.

claim: Regions with higher eccentricity have higher functional segregation from other networks in the rest of the brain, whereas regions with lower eccentricity have higher integration with other networks.
source: Under this framework, regions with higher eccentricity are interpreted as having higher functional segregation from other networks in the rest of the brain, whereas regions with lower eccentricity are interpreted as having higher integration (lower segregation) with other networks in the rest of the brain (Park et al., 2021a; Park et al., 2021b; Valk et al., 2023).
evidence: Directly stated interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: Baseline eccentricity is positively related to cortical node strength (r = 0.88, two-tailed p<0.001).
source: For instance, we find that baseline eccentricity is positively related to cortical node strength (r = 0.88, two-tailed p<0.001)
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with statistical significance.

claim: Baseline eccentricity is positively related to within-manifold degree z-score (r = 0.45, two-tailed p<0.001).
source: and within-manifold degree z-score (r = 0.45, two-tailed p<0.001)
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with statistical significance.

claim: Baseline eccentricity is negatively related to a region's participation coefficient (r = −0.74, two-tailed p<0.001).
source: Likewise, we find that baseline eccentricity is negatively related to a region's participation coefficient (r = −0.74, two-tailed p<0.001)
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with statistical significance.

claim: During early learning, several sensorimotor areas in the dorsal attention network exhibited increased covariance with areas of the salience/ventral attention network.
source: During early learning, we found that several sensorimotor areas in the dorsal attention network exhibited increased covariance with areas of the salience/ventral attention network
evidence: Directly stated result from the abstract.

claim: During early learning, several sensorimotor areas in the dorsal attention network exhibited reduced covariance with areas of the default mode network (DMN).
source: and reduced covariance with areas of the default mode network (DMN).
evidence: Directly stated result from the abstract.

claim: During late learning, sensorimotor areas exhibited increased covariance with DMN areas.
source: During late learning, these effects reversed, with sensorimotor areas now exhibiting increased covariance with DMN areas.
evidence: Directly stated result from the abstract.

claim: Areas in posteromedial cortex showed the opposite pattern across learning phases compared to other sensorimotor areas.
source: However, areas in posteromedial cortex showed the opposite pattern across learning phases, with its connectivity suggesting a role in coordinating activity across different networks over time.
evidence: Directly stated result from the abstract.

claim: The early > baseline contrast primarily revealed a pattern of increasing eccentricity (manifold expansion) across several brain regions.
source: This contrast primarily revealed a pattern of increasing eccentricity, that is, manifold expansion, across several brain regions, indicating that these regions became segregated from the rest of the brain (red areas in Figure 4A).
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: During early learning, regions showing manifold expansion included bilateral superior-parietal, somatomotor, supplementary motor, and premotor cortex, as well as regions in lateral visual cortex.
source: This included areas located throughout the cortical sensorimotor system and DAN, including bilateral superior-parietal, somatomotor, supplementary motor, and premotor cortex, as well as regions in lateral visual cortex.
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: During early learning, many key areas of the DMN exhibited manifold expansion, including bilateral medial frontal gyrus (MFG), MPFC, inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), and middle temporal cortex (MTC).
source: In addition, this contrast identified many key areas of the DMN, including bilateral medial frontal gyrus (MFG), MPFC, inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), and middle temporal cortex (MTC; for a network-level summary of these general effects, see the spider plot in Figure 4A).
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: During early learning, areas in the posterior medial cortex (PMC) and posterior angular gyrus (AG) exhibited a decrease in eccentricity (manifold contraction).
source: In contrast to this general pattern of expansion-related effects, we also found that a small subset of areas in the posterior medial cortex (PMC) and posterior angular gyrus (AG) instead exhibited a decrease in eccentricity, that is, manifold contraction (regions in blue in Figure 4A), indicating that these areas increased their integration with other areas of the brain.
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: No significant changes in striatal regions were observed from baseline to early learning.
source: Notably, we did not observe any significant changes in striatal regions from baseline to early learning
evidence: Directly stated null result.

claim: During late learning, several regions in bilateral MFG, MPFC, IFG, and MTC exhibited contraction along the manifold.
source: Specifically, during late learning, several regions in bilateral MFG, MPFC, IFG, and MTC now exhibited contraction along the manifold, indicating an increased integration of these areas with other regions of the brain
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: During late learning, areas in PMC and posterior AG exhibited expansion, indicating an increased segregation of these areas from the brain.
source: By contrast, areas in PMC and posterior AG now exhibited expansion, indicating an increased segregation of these areas from the brain.
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: During late learning, areas of the salience/ventral attention network, including the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and the anterior insula (AI), exhibited manifold expansion.
source: In addition, during late learning, we observed manifold expansion in several areas of the salience/ventral attention network (SalVentAttn), including the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and the anterior insula (AI)
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: No significant changes in striatal regions were observed from early to late learning.
source: Again, as in the early > baseline contrast, we did not observe any significant changes in striatal regions from early to late learning.
evidence: Directly stated null result.

claim: The right pallidum was the only striatal region that came close to reaching statistical significance (p=0.01) but did not pass whole-brain FDR correction (corrected alpha = 0.086).
source: The only region that came close to reaching statistical significance in the striatum was the right pallidum (p=0.01), but this region did not pass whole-brain FDR correction (corrected alpha = 0.086
evidence: Directly stated statistical result.

claim: During early learning, the left MPFC seed region exhibited increased connectivity with other DMN subregions and reduced connectivity with superior parietal and premotor areas in the DAN.
source: During early learning, we found that the left MPFC seed region, associated with the DMN network, exhibited increased connectivity with other DMN subregions and reduced connectivity with superior parietal and premotor areas in the DAN (Figure 5A).
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: During late learning, the MPFC exhibited increased connectivity with regions of the DAN but reduced connectivity with other DMN areas.
source: By contrast, during late learning, we observed a reversal in this pattern of connectivity changes, with the MPFC now exhibiting increased connectivity with the same regions of the DAN but reduced connectivity with other DMN areas.
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: The manifold expansion of the MPFC during early learning arises from its increased connectivity with other DMN areas (i.e., segregation of the DMN).
source: Together, these results suggest that the manifold expansion of the MPFC during early learning arises from its increased connectivity with other DMN areas (i.e., segregation of the DMN)
evidence: Directly stated interpretation of results.

claim: The manifold contraction of the MPFC during late learning arises from its increased connectivity with areas outside of the DMN, such as sensorimotor areas of the DAN.
source: whereas the manifold contraction of this region during late learning arises from its increased connectivity with areas outside of the DMN, such as sensorimotor areas of the DAN.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation of results.

claim: During early learning, the left PMd exhibited increased connectivity with other areas of the DAN and areas belonging to the SalVentAttn network, including the anterior insula/IFG, dACC, and inferior parietal cortex.
source: Specifically, during early learning, we observed increased connectivity of the left PMd with other areas of the DAN, as well as areas belonging to the SalVentAttn network, such as the anterior insula/IFG, dACC, and inferior parietal cortex.
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: During early learning, the left PMd exhibited decreased connectivity to DMN areas and the hippocampus.
source: Notably, this was coupled with its decreased connectivity to DMN areas and the hippocampus (Figure 5B).
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: During late learning, the left PMd exhibited increased connectivity with DMN areas and the hippocampus, whereas connectivity with the DAN and SalVentAttn areas decreased.
source: By contrast, during late learning, we observed a reversal in this pattern of effects, whereby connectivity with DMN areas and the hippocampus now increased, whereas connectivity with the DAN and SalVentAttn areas decreased.
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: During early learning, the left PMC seed region exhibited decreased connectivity with other DMN-A and Control-C subregions in bilateral PMC, as well as decreased connectivity with bilateral hippocampus and MPFC.
source: Finally, for the left PMC seed region, located at the border of the DMN-A and Control-C networks—and that was one of the few regions that exhibited contraction during early learning—we found that this region exhibited decreased connectivity during early learning with other DMN-A and Control-C subregions in bilateral PMC, as well as decreased connectivity with bilateral hippocampus and MPFC (Figure 5C).
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: During early learning, the left PMC exhibited increased connectivity with DAN areas in superior parietal cortex and premotor cortex, and most prominently, with areas in the anterior insula/IFG, dACC, and inferior parietal cortex (belonging to the SalVentAttn networks).
source: Instead, this PMC region exhibited increased connectivity with DAN areas in superior parietal cortex and premotor cortex, and most prominently, with areas in the anterior insula/IFG, dACC, and inferior parietal cortex (belonging to the SalVentAttn networks).
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: During late learning, the PMC seed region exhibited increased connectivity with other bilateral PMC areas, MPFC and the hippocampus, as well as reduced connectivity with the same DAN and SalVentAttn areas.
source: By contrast, during late learning, we again observed a reversal in this pattern of connectivity changes, with the PMC seed region now exhibiting increased connectivity with other bilateral PMC areas, MPFC and the hippocampus, as well as reduced connectivity with the same DAN and SalVentAttn areas.
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: Manifold contractions of the PMC during early learning arise from its increased integration with regions outside of the DMN-A and Control-C networks, such as the DAN and SalVentAttn.
source: Together, these results suggest that manifold contractions of the PMC during early learning arise from its increased integration with regions outside of the DMN-A and Control-C networks, such as the DAN and SalVentAttn
evidence: Directly stated interpretation of results.

claim: Manifold expansions of the PMC during late learning arise from its increased within-network connectivity with other DMN and Control areas (i.e., segregation).
source: whereas the manifold expansions of this region during late learning arise from its increased within-network connectivity with other DMN and Control areas (i.e., segregation).
evidence: Directly stated interpretation of results.

claim: During early learning, there is increased functional coupling between several sensorimotor areas of the DAN with areas of the SalVentAttn network.
source: Specifically, we find that, during early learning, there is increased functional coupling between several sensorimotor areas of the DAN with areas of the SalVentAttn network
evidence: Directly stated summary result.

claim: During late learning, DAN sensorimotor areas switch their connectivity to DMN areas.
source: whereas during late learning, these DAN sensorimotor areas switch their connectivity to DMN areas.
evidence: Directly stated summary result.

claim: Subjects exhibit significant variation in motor learning ability.
source: However, it is well established that subjects exhibit significant variation in motor learning ability (de Brouwer et al., 2018; de Brouwer et al., 2022; Standage et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: Functional principal component analysis (fPCA) was performed on subjects' learning curves to isolate the dominant patterns of variability in learning curves over time.
source: Using this fPCA approach, we found that a single component—encoding overall learning—captured the majority (~75%) of the variability in subjects' learning curves (Figure 6C).
evidence: Directly stated method and result with figure reference.

claim: A single component encoding overall learning captured approximately 75% of the variability in subjects' learning curves.
source: Using this fPCA approach, we found that a single component—encoding overall learning—captured the majority (~75%) of the variability in subjects' learning curves (Figure 6C).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with figure reference.

claim: The change in eccentricity of the DAN-A network correlated with learning score, such that the more the DAN-A network decreased in eccentricity from baseline to early learning, the better subjects performed at the task.
source: Using this permutation testing approach, we found that it was only the change in eccentricity of the DAN-A network that correlated with learning score (see Figure 7C), such that the more the DAN-A network decreased in eccentricity from baseline to early learning (i.e., contracted along the manifold), the better subjects performed at the task
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: During late learning, the more that the DAN-A network increased in eccentricity from early to late learning, the better subjects performed at the task.
source: Consistent with the notion that changes in the eccentricity of the DAN-A network are linked to learning performance, we also found the inverse pattern of effects during late learning, whereby the more that this same network increased in eccentricity from early to late learning (i.e., expanded along the manifold), the better subjects performed at the task (Figure 7D).
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: During early learning, DAN-A regions exhibited the largest increases in connectivity with one of the SalVentAttn subnetworks (SalVentAttn-B).
source: As can be observed in Figure 7E, we find that, during early learning, DAN-A regions exhibited the largest increases in connectivity with one of the SalVentAttn subnetworks (SalVentAttn-B)
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: During late learning, the DAN-A regions exhibited the largest increases in connectivity with one of the DMN subnetworks (DMN-B).
source: whereas, during late learning, the DAN-A regions exhibited the largest increases in connectivity with one of the DMN subnetworks (DMN-B).
evidence: Directly stated result.

claim: The transition in functional coupling between the DAN and SalVentAttn areas during early learning, to DAN and DMN areas during late learning, is associated with differences in subject performance.
source: These findings not only re-constitute the group-level effects reported above at the ROI level (in Figure 5), but they also suggest that this general transition in functional coupling—between the DAN and SalVentAttn areas during early learning, to DAN and DMN areas during late learning—is associated with differences in subject performance.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation of results.

claim: Neural systems anchored within the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) and striatum are important in evaluating whether the results of behavior are in line with expectations.
source: Numerous studies have shown that neural systems anchored within the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) and striatum are important in evaluating whether the results of behavior are in line with expectations (Averbeck and O'Doherty, 2022; Klein-Flügge et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2012; O'Doherty et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: When discrepancies arise between the expected versus actual results of an action—termed a 'prediction error'—this information serves as the teaching signal that can be used to update behavior directly.
source: Specifically, when discrepancies arise between the expected versus actual results of an action—termed a 'prediction error'—this information serves as the teaching signal that can be used to update behavior directly (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; O'Doherty et al., 2003; Samejima et al., 2005; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: The default mode network (DMN) was initially identified through its tendency to deactivate during cognitively demanding tasks.
source: Initially identified through its tendency to deactivate during cognitively demanding tasks, the DMN has traditionally been implicated in largely introspective, abstract cognitive functions such as autobiographical memory and internal mentation (Andrews‐Hanna et al., 2014; Binder et al., 2009; Christoff et al., 2016; Schacter et al., 2012; Spreng et al., 2009).
evidence: Directly stated historical characterization with supporting citations.

claim: Areas of the DMN are activated during demanding decision-making and working-memory tasks.
source: In recent years, however, this characterization of DMN activity has been difficult to reconcile, with an emerging body of functional MRI (fMRI) and neurophysiological evidence showing that areas of this network are activated during demanding decision-making and working-memory tasks (Foster et al., 2023; Hayden et al., 2009; Heilbronner and Platt, 2013; Murphy et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2018; Pearson et al., 2009; Vatansever et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: Each core region of the DMN is located in regions of association cortex that are equidistant between different primary systems.
source: One hypothesis concerning this system's function pertains to its unique topographic positioning on the cortical mantle (Smallwood et al., 2021): Each core region of the DMN is located in regions of association cortex that are equidistant between different primary systems
evidence: Directly stated hypothesis with citation.

claim: Posteromedial cortex, a key node of the DMN, is located precisely at the midpoint between the calcarine (visual) and central (motor) sulci.
source: for example, posteromedial cortex, a key node of the DMN, is located precisely at the midpoint between the calcarine (visual) and central (motor) sulci (Margulies et al., 2016).
evidence: Directly stated anatomical fact with citation.

claim: The unique topographic location of DMN regions is hypothesized to allow them broad oversight over distributed brain functions, enabling them to play a role in the coordination of activity across cortex.
source: This unique topographic location is hypothesized to allow DMN regions broad oversight over distributed brain functions, enabling them to play a role in the coordination of activity across cortex (Smallwood et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated hypothesis with citation.

claim: DMN areas such as medial frontal cortex and posteromedial cortex appear to play an important role in shifting between information gathering versus information exploitation during reward-guided decision-making tasks.
source: For instance, DMN areas such as medial frontal cortex and posteromedial cortex appear to play an important role in shifting between information gathering versus information exploitation during reward-guided decision-making tasks (Barack et al., 2017; Foster et al., 2023; Pearson et al., 2011; Pearson et al., 2009; Schuck et al., 2015; Trudel et al., 2021)—the so-called explore/exploit trade-off (Frank et al., 2009; Sutton and Barto, 2018).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: The DMN supports behavior under conditions in which performance depends on knowledge accrued across several trials rather than by immediate sensory inputs.
source: Consistent with this, recent studies have argued that broad features of the DMN's activity can be explained under the auspices that it supports behavior under conditions in which performance depends on knowledge accrued across several trials rather than by immediate sensory inputs (Hayden et al., 2008; Murphy et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2018; Vatansever et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: Connectivity between DMN regions and sensorimotor cortex is altered when normal visual-motor contingencies governing behavior are interrupted over the course of several trials.
source: Extending these ideas, we recently showed that the DMN plays a role in motor adaptation, showing that connectivity between DMN regions and sensorimotor cortex is altered when normal visual-motor contingencies governing behavior are interrupted over the course of several trials (Gale et al., 2022).
evidence: Directly stated prior finding with citation.

claim: High-dimensional neural population activity can be described along a low-dimensional subspace or manifold.
source: This approach builds on recent electrophysiological studies in macaques, demonstrating that high-dimensional neural population activity can be described along a low-dimensional subspace or manifold (Cunningham and Yu, 2014; Gallego et al., 2017; Shenoy et al., 2013; Vyas et al., 2020)
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: The manifold approach has provided key insights into the overarching structural and functional architecture of the human brain.
source: This same organizational structure also appears to govern the macroscale activity of cortex, with this manifold approach having recently provided key insights into the overarching structural and functional architecture of the human brain (Huntenburg et al., 2018; Paquola et al., 2019; Shine et al., 2019a; Shine et al., 2019b; Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: Areas within the SalVentAttn network have been implicated in several aspects of cognitive control and motivation.
source: In other work, areas within the SalVentAttn network have been implicated in several aspects of cognitive control and motivation (Botvinick et al., 2004; Holroyd and Yeung, 2012; Pearson et al., 2009; Shenhav et al., 2014)
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: SalVentAttn regions are thought to support exploratory behavior in reward-based decision-making.
source: and in studies on reward-based decision-making, these regions are thought to support exploratory behavior.
evidence: Directly stated claim.

claim: SalVentAttn areas are activated in response to novel or salient stimuli in the environment, presumably reflecting the engagement of attentional resources for sampling new information.
source: For instance, several neuroimaging studies have shown that SalVentAttn areas are activated in response to novel or salient stimuli in the environment, presumably reflecting the engagement of attentional resources for sampling new information (Corbetta et al., 2008).
evidence: Directly stated claim with citation.

claim: Several SalVentAttn areas are implicated in information gathering functions to optimize reward outcomes.
source: In addition, recent work (Badre et al., 2012; Blanchard and Gershman, 2018; Boorman et al., 2009; Daw et al., 2006; Hogeveen et al., 2022; Kolling et al., 2016) implicates several SalVentAttn areas in information gathering functions, so as to optimize reward outcomes.
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: During the early phases of reward-guided learning, performance is more variable, presumably as individuals explore the relationship between motor commands and associated sensory feedback.
source: This neural perspective is consistent with both others' (Dam et al., 2013) and our own behavioral findings (de Brouwer et al., 2022) that, during the early phases of reward-guided learning, performance is more variable, presumably as individuals explore the relationship between motor commands and associated sensory feedback.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: Connectivity between the DMN and premotor cortex tends to increase once rules have been learned.
source: This interpretation is consistent with prior work showing that connectivity between the DMN and premotor cortex tends to increase once rules have been learned (Shamloo and Helie, 2016)
evidence: Directly stated claim with citation.

claim: The DMN contributes to behavior when actions must be guided by information from memory and a knowledge of task structure.
source: as well as studies from other task domains showing that the DMN contributes to behavior when actions must be guided by information from memory and a knowledge of task structure (Murphy et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2018; Vatansever et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: Functional interactions between the DMN and brain regions involved in sensorimotor processes support a mode of action in which behavior must be guided by memory processes.
source: Our analysis, therefore, provides additional evidence, albeit from the domain of human motor learning, that functional interactions between the DMN and brain regions involved in sensorimotor processes support a mode of action in which behavior must be guided by memory processes (Smallwood et al., 2021)—in this case, the history of reward information accrued across previous movement trajectories.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation with citation.

claim: The PMC contains echoes of neural signals originating from across the cortex.
source: Although traditionally considered a member of the DMN (Thomas Yeo et al., 2011), studies have established that the PMC contains echoes of neural signals originating from across the cortex (Leech et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated claim with citations.

claim: Areas within the PMC are linked to reward processing.
source: Prior studies have linked the activity of PMC areas to reward processing (Kable and Glimcher, 2007; Knutson and Bossaerts, 2007; McCoy and Platt, 2005)
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: Areas within the PMC are linked to the selection of response strategies that attempt to optimize reward outcomes.
source: and the selection of response strategies that attempt to optimize reward outcomes (Barack et al., 2017; Pearson et al., 2009; Wan et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: Areas within the PMC are able to integrate information over particularly long periods of time.
source: Consistent with this, recent research shows that areas within the PMC are able to integrate information over particularly long periods of time (Hasson et al., 2015; Heilbronner and Platt, 2013; Lerner et al., 2011).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: The PMC is an ideal candidate region to orchestrate the neural transition from exploring the relationship between motor commands and sensory feedback during early learning to subsequently exploiting this learned relationship during late learning.
source: This characteristic positions the PMC as an ideal candidate region to orchestrate the neural transition from (1) exploring the relationship between motor commands and sensory feedback during early learning to (2) subsequently exploiting this learned relationship during late learning.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation based on prior evidence.

claim: The PMC plays an important role in directing long-term behavioral adaptation in accordance with higher-order task objectives.
source: Taken together, these distinctive functional properties of PMC activity, coupled with its diverse patterns of whole-brain connectivity (Hagmann et al., 2008; Hutchison et al., 2015; Margulies et al., 2009), suggest an important role for this region in directing long-term behavioral adaptation in accordance with higher-order task objectives (Braga et al., 2013; Pearson et al., 2011).
evidence: Directly stated interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: The relatively small size of the striatum may mean that the analysis approach was too coarse to identify changes in the connectivity of this region.
source: First, the relatively small size of the striatum may mean that our analysis approach was too coarse to identify changes in the connectivity of this region.
evidence: Directly stated speculation about methodological limitation.

claim: Areas such as the hippocampus and caudate are not homogeneous areas but themselves exhibit gradients of connectivity that can only be revealed at the voxel level.
source: For example, areas such the hippocampus and caudate are not homogeneous areas but themselves exhibit gradients of connectivity (e.g., head versus tail) that can only be revealed at the voxel level (Tian et al., 2020; Vos de Wael et al., 2021).
evidence: Directly stated claim with supporting citations.

claim: The low-dimensional manifold architecture in cortex did not strongly depend on whether or not striatal regions were included in the analysis.
source: Consistent with this perspective, we found that the low-dimensional manifold architecture in cortex did not strongly depend on whether or not striatal regions were included in the analysis (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated result with figure reference.

claim: Preprocessing of anatomical and functional MRI data was performed using fMRIPrep 20.1.1.
source: Preprocessing of anatomical and functional MRI data was performed using fMRIPrep 20.1.1 (Esteban et al., 2019, Esteban et al., 2024; RRID:SCR_016216)
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing method with citations.

claim: fMRIPrep is based on Nipype 1.5.0.
source: which is based on Nipype 1.5.0 (Gorgolewski et al., 2011; Gorgolewski et al., 2018; RRID:SCR_002502).
evidence: Directly stated software dependency with citations.

claim: T1w images were corrected for intensity non-uniformity (INU) with N4BiasFieldCorrection, distributed with ANTs 2.2.0.
source: T1w images were corrected for intensity non-uniformity (INU) with N4BiasFieldCorrection (Tustison et al., 2010), distributed with ANTs 2.2.0 (Avants et al., 2008; RRID:SCR_004757).
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step with citations.

claim: Brain tissue segmentation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), white matter (WM), and gray matter (GM) was performed on the brain-extracted T1w using FAST (FSL 5.0.9).
source: Brain tissue segmentation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), white matter (WM), and gray matter (GM) was performed on the brain-extracted T1w using fast (FSL 5.0.9, RRID:SCR_002823)(Zhang et al., 2001).
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step with citation.

claim: Brain surfaces were reconstructed using recon-all (FreeSurfer 6.0.1).
source: Brain surfaces were reconstructed using recon-all (FreeSurfer 6.0.1, RRID:SCR_001847; Dale et al., 1999)
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step with citation.

claim: Volume-based spatial normalization to standard space (MNI152NLin6Asym) was performed through nonlinear registration with antsRegistration (ANTs 2.2.0).
source: Volume-based spatial normalization to standard space (MNI152NLin6Asym) was performed through nonlinear registration with antsRegistration (ANTs 2.2.0)
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step.

claim: Head-motion parameters were estimated before any spatiotemporal filtering using mcflirt (FSL 5.0.9).
source: Head-motion parameters with respect to the BOLD reference (transformation matrices, and six corresponding rotation and translation parameters) are estimated before any spatiotemporal filtering using mcflirt (FSL 5.0.9; Jenkinson et al., 2002).
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step with citation.

claim: BOLD runs were slice-time corrected using 3dTshift from AFNI 20160207.
source: BOLD runs were slice-time corrected using 3dTshift from AFNI 20160207 (Cox and Hyde, 1997; RRID:SCR_005927).
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step with citation.

claim: The BOLD reference was co-registered to the T1w reference using bbregister (FreeSurfer) which implements boundary-based registration.
source: The BOLD reference was then co-registered to the T1w reference using bbregister (FreeSurfer) which implements boundary-based registration (Greve and Fischl, 2009).
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step with citation.

claim: A set of 34 motion and physiological regressors were extracted to mitigate the impact of head motion and physiological noise.
source: A set of 34 motion and physiological regressors were extracted in order to mitigate the impact of head motion and physiological noise.
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step.

claim: The six head-motion estimates were expanded to include temporal derivatives and quadratic terms, totaling 24 head-motion parameters.
source: The six head-motion estimates calculated in the correction step were expanded to include temporal derivatives and quadratic terms of each of the original and derivative regressors, totaling 24 head-motion parameters (Satterthwaite et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step with citation.

claim: Ten component-based physiological regressors were estimated using the aCompCor approach.
source: Ten component-based physiological regressors were estimated using the aCompCor approach (Behzadi et al., 2007; Muschelli et al., 2014), where the top five PCs were separately extracted from WM and CSF masks.
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step with citations.

claim: Region time series were denoised using confound regressors in conjunction with discrete cosine regressors (128 s cut-off for high-pass filtering) and low-pass filtering using a Butterworth filter (100 s cut-off).
source: Region time series were denoised using the above-mentioned confound regressors in conjunction with the discrete cosine regressors (128 s cut-off for high-pass filtering) produced from fMRIprep and low-pass filtering using a Butterworth filter (100 s cut-off) implemented in Nilearn.
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step.

claim: All region time series were z-scored.
source: Finally, all region time series were z-scored.
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step.

claim: The first six imaging volumes were discarded to avoid scanner equilibrium effects.
source: For every participant, region time series from the task scans were spliced into three equal-lengthed task epochs (210 imaging volumes each), after having discarded the first six imaging volumes (thus avoiding scanner equilibrium effects).
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing step.

claim: Functional connectivity matrices were estimated using the Ledoit–Wolf estimator.
source: Then, we separately estimated functional connectivity matrices for each epoch by computing the region-wise covariance matrices using the Ledoit–Wolf estimator (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004).
evidence: Directly stated method with citation.

claim: Equal-length epochs for the three phases ensured that no biases in covariance estimation were introduced due to differences in time-series length.
source: Note that our use of equal-length epochs for the three phases ensured that no biases in covariance estimation were introduced due to differences in time-series length.
evidence: Directly stated methodological rationale.

claim: Row-wise thresholding was applied to retain the top 10% connections in each row before computing cosine similarity.
source: First, consistent with previous studies (Gale et al., 2022; Hong et al., 2020; Margulies et al., 2016; Vos de Wael et al., 2020), we applied row-wise thresholding to retain the top 10% connections in each row, and then computed cosine similarity between each row to produce an affinity matrix that describes the similarity of each region's connectivity profiles.
evidence: Directly stated method with citations.

claim: PCA was selected as the dimension reduction technique based on recent work demonstrating the improved reliability of PCA over nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques.
source: We selected PCA as our dimension reduction technique based on recent work demonstrating the improved reliability of PCA over nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., diffusion map embedding; Hong et al., 2020).
evidence: Directly stated methodological choice with citation.

claim: All individual manifolds were aligned to the baseline template manifold using Procrustes alignment.
source: We aligned all individual manifolds (36 participants × 3 epochs; 108 total) to this baseline template manifold using Procrustes alignment.
evidence: Directly stated method.

claim: Across participants and epochs, the top three PCs, following Procrustes alignment, had an average correlation of r = 0.88 with their respective PCs in the template manifold.
source: Across participants and epochs, the top three PCs, following Procrustes alignment, had an average correlation of r = 0.88 with their respective PCs in the template manifold, thus demonstrating good overall reliability and alignment across participants and epochs.
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result.

claim: FDR correction (q < 0.05) was applied across regions for each contrast when comparing region eccentricity between epochs.
source: We applied FDR correction (q < 0.05) across regions for each contrast.
evidence: Directly stated statistical correction method.

claim: The statistical significance of network-level correlations was tested by building null models that account for the spatial autocorrelation in the brain maps.
source: We tested the statistical significance of these network-level correlations by building null models that account for the spatial autocorrelation in the brain maps (Markello et al., 2022; Váša et al., 2018; see 'Materials and methods')
evidence: Directly stated statistical method with citations.

claim: The study establishes the neural changes that support reward-based motor learning.
source: Our results establish the neural changes that support reward-based motor learning and identify distinct transitions in the functional coupling of sensorimotor to transmodal cortex when adapting behavior.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from the abstract.
